title: Feedback That Changes What Happens Next
performance: The viewer takes one real piece of feedback they have been putting off and reshapes it into a specific observed behaviour, its effect, and a clear request for next time, with a way to check back, ready to say this week.

audience.assumed_prior: Knows feedback matters. Has given or received the vague kind and watched nothing change. Does not yet have a repeatable way to say it differently.
audience.why: Corporate employees who give feedback to peers or direct reports. Prior knowledge is the only branch: they know the problem, so the lesson spends little time on why feedback matters and moves quickly to rebuilding a sentence.
audience.motivation: Get a colleague to actually do something different without damaging the working relationship.
audience.context: One-to-one, spoken feedback between peers or from manager to direct report. Not performance reviews, formal discipline or written feedback.

strategy.name: worked_example_led
strategy.rationale: The brief supplies one running example, a manager and a teammate after a tense meeting. Practitioners benefit from seeing the weak sentence rebuilt one part at a time, then fading to their own sentence. The three parts are a short procedure, so a single worked example carries it and a named model is not needed.
strategy.signature_move: Show the weak sentence, test it against the camera, rebuild one part at a time on the board, compare versions, then hand over the viewer's own sentence.

misconceptions.belief: If the tone is kind and the colleague nods and agrees, the feedback worked.
misconceptions.why_tempting: Warmth feels safe for the relationship, and a nod feels like understanding. Both are visible in the moment.

misconceptions.belief: Saying what you think of someone's attitude, such as 'you were being dismissive', is honest, direct feedback.
misconceptions.why_tempting: It is how the speaker experienced the moment, so it feels truthful. But it is an interpretation of motive, and the speaker can be wrong about it.

misconceptions.belief: A request is enough if it only says what to stop.
misconceptions.why_tempting: Stopping the problem is the obvious goal, so naming the thing to stop feels complete. It leaves a gap about what to do instead.

hook.sketch: Say a manager tells a teammate after a tense meeting, 'You need to be more professional.' The teammate nods warmly, and the next meeting goes exactly the same way. On screen: a nod, then the same tense meeting again.

arc.promise: You will leave able to rebuild that same sentence so your colleague can act on it, and the kind tone was never the problem.
arc.bridge_from_prior: You have watched this happen, or done it: a kind, agreed-with conversation and then no change. Start from that, and show what the sentence actually handed over.

sections.goal: the viewer can explain why a kind, vague sentence leaves the listener with a feeling but nothing to repeat or stop
concepts: Vague feedback gives a judgement but no action (F2)
A nod and agreement is a weak sign anything will change (F4)
Kind tone shapes how it feels, content decides what the listener can change (F14)
Character labels are often heard as an attack (F3)

sections.goal: the viewer can use the camera test to replace a label with what anyone watching would have seen or heard
concepts: Observable behaviour: what a camera would have seen or heard, what was said, when, to whom (F5)
Attitude, motive and intent are interpretations the speaker can be wrong about (F6)
Name a specific moment, not a general label (F7)

sections.goal: the viewer can apply the effect step by stating what the behaviour did to the work or the team, from something that actually happened or that they directly felt
concepts: The effect tells the listener why it matters beyond the speaker's opinion (F8)
Own reaction as a stated effect is more honest and harder to dispute (F9)
Do not speculate about what others think (F8)

sections.goal: the viewer can build a request that names a specific action for next time and agrees a way to check back
concepts: A clear request names a specific action for next time (F10)
Say what to do instead, not only what to stop (F11)
Agree a time or moment to talk again, which makes it more likely the request is remembered and noticed (F12)
Soon after the event is usually most useful, though sometimes waiting for calm or privacy is wiser (F15)

sections.goal: the viewer can distinguish the version that names a behaviour, an effect and a request from the versions that fail, and say why each fails
concepts: Three versions aimed at the same teammate: warm but vague, a character judgement with a stop-only demand, and the full behaviour, effect and request
Each failure maps to a part missing or a label standing in for observation

sections.goal: the viewer can carry out the three parts on one real conversation they have been avoiding, and shape its opening line like the running example
concepts: Pick one real conversation
Behaviour, effect and request is one common shape; other models exist and are also used (F13)
Check each part with the camera test and the specific-action test

sections.goal: the viewer can describe what the colleague now knows to do in the next meeting, and what visibly changes
concepts: Return to the opening meeting with the rebuilt sentence
The colleague has something specific to do, and the follow-up moment arrives
No guarantee of change; the structure makes change easier to see and to ask for

arc.payoff: Back in the opening meeting, the manager says the rebuilt sentence: 'In today's meeting you interrupted Sam twice while she was presenting. I lost track of her point. Next meeting, please let her finish before you respond, and let's talk after it.' The teammate now has something to do. The next meeting visibly goes differently, and the viewer is handed their own sentence to say this week.

practice_ladder.description: The presenter rebuilds 'be more professional' on the board one part at a time, narrating the camera test, then the effect, then the request.
The viewer first supplies the observable version of the label before it is shown, then picks the complete version out of three about the same colleague.
The viewer drafts the opening line of a real conversation in the same three-part shape, using the running example as the pattern.

recall_moments.prompt: Before the effect appears: 'You need to be more professional.' What would a camera have seen in that meeting? Say it as what was done, when, and to whom, then check against the board.
Three versions for the same teammate. Which one names a behaviour, an effect and a request?
recall_moments.answer: The version that names the specific moment (interrupted Sam twice while she was presenting), the effect (I lost track of the point), and a request for next time (let her finish before you respond, and talk after).
recall_moments.tempting_wrong: The warm, appreciative version that asks them to be more careful about how they come across, because a kind tone keeps the relationship safe.

recall_moments.prompt: Without looking back: what is the camera test, and which part of the sentence does it protect?

transfer_tasks: Pick one piece of feedback you have been putting off for a peer or direct report. Draft its opening line as a behaviour, an effect and a request, apply the camera test to the first part, and say it this week, agreeing a moment to check back.

gagne.attention: arc.hook (scenario: the nod, then the same meeting again)
gagne.recall_prior: arc.bridge_from_prior and section bridge (viewer has given or received vague feedback)
gagne.guidance: practice_ladder worked rung and recall_moments pause_predict after behaviour
gagne.practice: section check, quiz recall moment, section apply

merrill.task: The running example, a manager and a teammate after a tense meeting, introduced in the hook
merrill.activation: Section bridge, then the viewer's own experience of vague feedback
merrill.demonstration: Sections behaviour, effect, request, with the rebuild on the board
merrill.integration: Section apply plus transfer_tasks, saying the line this week

mayer.note: One loud thing on screen at a time; the sentence on the board is built piece by piece; the spoken narration carries the explanation while the board holds only the sentence and the named rule; no decorative extras.

arcs.relevance: promise: rebuild the same sentence, the kind tone was never the problem
arcs.confidence: worked rebuild, then faded check, then independent draft
arcs.satisfaction: payoff returns to the opening meeting, handled

framework_audit.bloom_path: understand -> apply -> apply -> apply -> analyze -> apply -> understand

flags: DURATION-MISMATCH: no requested length was visible in the input, so 600 s was chosen to fit the brief's nine arc roles, including the optional bridge and apply. The apply section is a rest section over 180 s because the viewer drafts their own line while the screen stays calm.

Not verified: no source material exists for the knowledge sheet (topic mode, needs human review). All example wording is illustrative, written for this lesson. Sam and the manager and teammate are invented scenario characters, framed as 'say'.

Open question from the brief resolved: the three parts are taught in plain words and F13 notes that other models exist; no named model is taught. No industry was given, so a generic office is assumed.
